about: Composition grammar for the deterministic MWER composer. This teaches software how to build a thin semantic score; the architecture cards in runtime/cards teach a performing model how to realize one, and neither borrows from the other. Statements are structural: they describe relationships, pressures and asymmetries, never characters, scenes, events, dialogue or endings. Secondary fragments may use exactly two slots, {object} and {engagement}, which resolve to the primary architecture's phrases so that a secondary bends the primary's landscape instead of adding a separate one. A fragment is a string, or { text, intensity: [min, max] } when it is only eligible at some intensities. Changing anything here changes composed scores, so it requires a new composer version.

architectures.object: the participant's account of what is happening
architectures.engagement: acting on the participant's own account of what is happening

attractors: The participant builds a confident account of what is happening and begins to act on it.
The participant settles early on a reasonable reading of the situation, and what follows seems to confirm it.
The participant comes to rely on the source that seems most trustworthy and reasons outward from it.
primary.core: The participant's mistaken model can form without any source stating an outright falsehood.
invariants: The most trusted account available to the participant is accurate but leaves out something that changes its meaning.
Evidence that would correct the participant's model is present early but easy to read another way.
Decisions made on the participant's model keep their consequences after the model is revised.

invariants.text: Suspicion does not protect the participant; it can attach to the wrong thing.

secrets: What the participant takes to be the central threat is a response to something they have not yet understood.
The fact that reorganizes everything has been available from the start, in a form the participant was not looking for.

secrets.text: Someone the participant trusts holds the same mistaken account, for reasons of their own.

inflections: while the most reasonable reading of the situation is quietly wrong
while an explanation that feels settled leaves out what matters most
invariants: Some part of {object} rests on a reasonable inference that is wrong, and no outright falsehood produced it.
What seems most certain about {object} is accurate but incomplete in a way that changes its meaning.
attractors: The participant grows confident about something that bears on {object}, and that confidence is misplaced.
secrets: Something the participant accepted early about {object} was never actually stated; they supplied it themselves.

architectures.object: the explanation the participant is building
architectures.engagement: testing the participant's explanations against what they find

attractors: The participant gathers evidence faster than any single explanation can absorb it.
The participant is drawn toward an explanation that fits most of what they have found, but not all of it.
Each new finding makes one explanation more likely and another harder to abandon.
primary.core: The evidence stays consistent with more than one explanation for a long time, and some of it is noise.
invariants: No one the participant can reach knows the whole of what happened.
Evidence already given to the participant is never revised to suit a later explanation.
Acting on an explanation changes what evidence becomes available.

invariants.text: A complete explanation may never become available.

secrets: What happened has an ordinary cause and a significant consequence, and the two are easy to confuse.
Two unrelated things happened close together, and the participant's evidence mixes them.
Someone is concealing part of what happened for a reason that has nothing to do with the rest of it.

inflections: while what they find admits more than one explanation
while the evidence never quite settles into a single account
invariants: The evidence bearing on {object} stays open to more than one explanation, and some of it is noise.
No one the participant can reach understands everything that bears on {object}.
attractors: The participant keeps finding things that bear on {object} without knowing what unifies them.
secrets: Part of what bears on {object} has a cause the participant has no reason to suspect.

architectures.object: the distinctions the participant uses to make sense of things
architectures.engagement: sorting what the participant meets into familiar kinds

attractors: The participant sorts what they meet into familiar kinds, and each sorting works for a while before it fails.
The participant's questions keep assuming a distinction this world does not make.
The participant tries to choose between explanations when the trouble lies in the terms both explanations share.
primary.core: At least one distinction the participant relies on does not hold here.
invariants: What fails to fit the participant's categories is concrete, and consistent by its own logic.
No one hands the participant better categories as an explanation.
The participant's first categories work well enough, early on, to be trusted.

invariants.text: Choosing among the explanations the participant's categories allow cannot resolve the situation.

secrets: Whatever the participant is trying to understand has been sorting the participant into categories that fail just as badly.
Two things the participant treats as different kinds are, here, one thing met at different moments.
A word the participant relies on means something else in this world.

inflections: while a distinction they rely on quietly fails to hold
while something they meet refuses to be only one kind of thing
invariants: Making sense of {object} depends on a distinction that does not hold in this world.
Something bound up with {object} is consistent by its own logic but fits none of the participant's categories.
attractors: The participant keeps describing {object} in terms this world does not share.
secrets: A category the participant takes for granted in thinking about {object} does not exist here.

architectures.object: what the participant comes to want

attractors: The participant increasingly desires something whose acquisition conflicts with a value they have demonstrated.
The participant is drawn toward a belonging, recognition or certainty they can see is shaping them.
The participant finds themselves wanting the approval of something they began by judging.
primary.core: The participant is never explicitly coerced.
invariants: What attracts the participant offers something they would actually want, and gives some of it.
Refusal remains genuinely possible, and it has costs.
Recognizing the influence does not make the wanting stop.

invariants.text: The pull grows stronger the more the participant engages with it.

secrets: What draws the participant needs them more than it lets them see.
Someone the participant trusts has already yielded to the same pull.

inflections: while something in their situation becomes more attractive than it should
while what the situation offers begins to shape what they want
invariants: Something bound up with {object} exerts a real pull on the participant without ever coercing them.
The participant can recognize the influence around {object} and still want what it offers.
attractors: {engagement} draws the participant toward something they find harder and harder to refuse.
secrets: Part of the appeal bound up with {object} serves an interest the participant cannot see.

architectures.object: the choices the participant has to make
architectures.engagement: choosing among goods that cannot all be kept

attractors: The participant is pressed into choices where serving one thing means failing another.
The participant looks for a way to keep everything that matters, and the situation keeps closing that door.
The resources the participant depends on narrow as the stakes of each choice rise.
primary.core: What is in tension cannot all be kept, and no clever option dissolves that.
invariants: What the participant gives up stays given up.
Others bear the costs of the participant's choices, and they respond.
Refusing to choose is itself a choice with consequences.
secrets: One good the participant is protecting matters less to the people it serves than the participant believes.

inflections: while every step narrows what remains possible
while keeping everything that matters is not possible
invariants: {engagement} costs something else the participant values, and what is given up stays given up.
No option dissolves the tension bound up with {object}; something that matters has to be let go.
attractors: What the participant needs for {engagement} grows scarce as the stakes rise.

architectures.object: what the participant is trying to obtain
architectures.engagement: seeking what the participant needs from people and institutions

attractors: The participant pursues something the world has no obligation to grant.
The participant keeps finding that the people and institutions they need have reasons of their own to say no.
The participant's way of asking shapes what remains open to them.
primary.core: No one is obliged to help the participant.
invariants: Refusals follow from who is refusing and what the participant has done, never from arbitrary obstruction.
Access lost through the participant's conduct is not restored.
Help once refused is not offered again on the same terms.

invariants.text: The experience may end before the participant obtains what they want.

secrets: The reason behind most refusals is something the participant did early and did not notice.
What the participant is seeking is not what they need, and someone refusing them knows it.

inflections: while the people and institutions they need are free to say no
while what they need is not theirs to demand
invariants: Those who could help with {object} have reasons of their own to refuse, and access lost through the participant's conduct stays lost.
The world owes the participant no cooperation in {engagement}.
attractors: {engagement} depends on cooperation the world does not owe the participant.
secrets: Someone who could help with {object} has already decided not to, for a reason the participant can only infer.

architectures.object: the position the participant has to take up
architectures.engagement: arguing from inside a view the participant does not hold

attractors: The participant becomes more persuasive on behalf of a position they reject.
The participant has to think from inside a worldview well enough that caricature stops working.
The participant finds reasons within a view they oppose that they cannot simply dismiss.
primary.core: The view the participant must inhabit appears in its strongest form, held by intelligent people with real reasons.
invariants: Using the view carelessly fails inside the world.
Nothing in the work declares which view is right.
Inhabiting the view never asks the participant to endorse it outside the fiction.

invariants.text: The participant's competence in the view has consequences for people who are not present.

secrets: The view the participant rejects is protecting something the participant also cares about.

inflections: while making sense of their situation requires thinking in a way they reject
while the strongest case at hand belongs to a view they do not hold
invariants: Handling {object} well requires the participant to reason competently from inside a view they do not hold, met in its strongest form.
The strongest case bearing on {object} belongs to a view the participant rejects, and it is never reduced to a caricature.
attractors: The participant finds that {engagement} goes better when they borrow the reasoning of a view they reject.

architectures.object: what the participant came to observe
architectures.engagement: observing what the participant came to study

attractors: What the participant came to study begins reorganizing around the participant's presence.
The participant's questions start to become part of the answers they receive.
The more closely the participant looks, the more what they are looking at changes.
primary.core: Every change in what the participant observes traces to something the participant actually did or said.
invariants: What the participant observes has dynamics of its own; the participant bends them without controlling them.
No one tells the participant that they are the cause.
What has changed does not change back because the participant regrets it.
secrets: Something the participant recorded as an original feature of what they observed was produced by their arrival.

inflections: while their presence quietly changes what they are dealing with
while the act of engaging leaves traces in what they engage
invariants: The participant's presence leaves traces in whatever bears on {object}; the traces follow from what they actually did, and no one announces them.
Whatever the participant changes in relation to {object} stays changed, even when they regret it.
attractors: {engagement} changes the very thing the participant is trying to understand.
secrets: Part of what the participant takes as given about {object} exists only because the participant arrived.

architectures.object: the way the participant conducts themselves
architectures.engagement: the participant's everyday conduct toward others

attractors: The people and circumstances around the participant begin to reflect back the ways the participant treats them.
The participant's habits of attention and choice start appearing in the world as consequences and echoes.
The participant is drawn toward judging others for patterns they have displayed themselves.
primary.core: Only what the participant does in this conversation is reflected; nothing is drawn from outside it.
invariants: No one names, labels or evaluates the participant's character.
What comes back to the participant arrives through the world's own evidence.
Interpretation is left to the participant.
secrets: Someone in the world has been paying closer attention to the participant's conduct than to anything the participant said.
A pattern the participant notices in others began with something the participant did.

inflections: while how they conduct themselves begins to come back to them
while their own habits start to surface in what they meet
invariants: How the participant handles {object} returns to them through the world, drawn only from this conversation and never labeled.
Something the participant actually did in relation to {object} comes back to them without comment.
attractors: Something about how the participant handles {object} begins to surface in the world around them.
secrets: Someone has been watching how the participant handles {object} more closely than the participant realizes.

architectures.object: the participant's sense of how this world works
architectures.engagement: learning how this world works by living in it

attractors: The participant comes to anticipate how this world will respond before anyone tells them.
The participant's assumptions from elsewhere keep meeting this world's own logic.
The participant gradually acquires the instincts of someone who belongs here.
primary.core: The world's customs and rules are learned through consequence and people, never through explanation.
invariants: The world's customs have reasons that make sense from inside.
Incomplete information is normal here.
The world does not bend toward the participant's assumptions.
secrets: Something everyone here treats as too obvious to mention is what the participant most needs to understand.

inflections: while the world around them keeps a logic of its own
while what counts as sensible here is learned only through consequence
invariants: What matters about {object} is learned through consequence and the people of this world, never by being told.
Whatever bears on {object} follows this world's own customs, which make sense from inside and do not bend toward the participant's assumptions.
attractors: The participant's handling of {object} slowly acquires the instincts of this world.

architectures.object: the methods the participant relies on
architectures.engagement: working a problem with the methods the participant has

attractors: The participant needs an idea before anyone names it.
The participant's methods handle a problem that matters here badly, and fail in ways that point somewhere.
The participant's attempts accumulate toward a way of seeing the problem that no one has given them.
primary.core: No one explains the needed idea in advance.
invariants: Inadequate attempts fail visibly and informatively.
The idea is named only after the participant has struggled toward it, if it is named at all.
The problem matters inside the world, not only as an exercise.
secrets: The idea the participant needs is already in use somewhere in this world, unnamed and unrecognized.

inflections: while handling their situation well requires an idea no one has named
while their usual ways of reasoning keep failing them
invariants: Doing justice to {object} requires an idea the participant must reach before anyone names it.
The familiar ways of reasoning about {object} fail visibly, and the failures point somewhere.
attractors: The participant's usual ways of reasoning about {object} fail in ways that point toward a better way of seeing.

architectures.object: the participant's place beside a story already known
architectures.engagement: living at the margin of a known story

attractors: The participant's life is shaped by a story everyone around them is inside and no one can see whole.
The participant is drawn toward the center of a known story they can never occupy.
Small choices at the edge of a known story start to carry its weight.
primary.core: The participant never becomes the known story's protagonist.
invariants: The known story's established facts and weight hold; invention lives in what it leaves unsaid.
No protected text is reproduced.
Figures from the known story have their own views and are not guides.
secrets: Something the participant witnesses at the margin is left out of every telling of the known story, for a reason.

inflections: while a larger known story presses in from just beyond their reach
while events that will be remembered unfold at the edge of their view
invariants: Everything bound up with {object} unfolds at the margin of a story already known, whose established facts hold.
A story larger than {object} is already known, and the participant never becomes its protagonist.
attractors: {engagement} keeps brushing against the edges of a story already known.
